guide.title: Shock in Trauma
guide.lead: In trauma, shock means bleeding until proven otherwise. Stop the bleeding, keep the patient warm, and give just enough fluid to keep a radial pulse. A head injury needs a higher BP. Don't miss the shocks that need a needle or a surgeon rather than fluid.

sections.title: How much blood is gone?
rows: Tachycardia, anxiety, narrowed pulse pressure; BP maintained
Lethargic, very low BP: about to arrest

steps.title: Go
steps.text: Rapid transport and pre-alert; IV/IO access en route.

steps.title: Permissive fluids
steps.text: Small boluses (about 250 mL) to a radial pulse or systolic 80–90 mmHg; blood where available; avoid large volumes of crystalloid.

steps.title: Head injury?
steps.text: No permissive hypotension: systolic at least 110 mmHg in most adults.

sections.title: Shock that fluid won't fix
rows: Absent breath sounds one side, distended neck veins, hypoxia
Muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins, equal breath sounds
Bradycardia, warm dry skin, cord injury
Fluids, vasopressors, atropine (ALS); still look for bleeding

quiz.q: Stab wound to the right upper quadrant: BP 106/70, HR 118, pale and sweaty, anxious. Class?
GCS 10 after a crash, BP 120/70, deformed thigh. Fluid target?
options: Avoid hypotension: systolic at least 110 mmHg

quiz.q: BP 86/54, HR 112, warm dry legs, cool arms, no sensation below the nipples. Shock type?
options: Neurogenic, from a thoracic cord injury

quiz.explanation: Enough to perfuse without blowing off clots.

quiz.q: Why avoid large volumes of crystalloid in bleeding?
options: They dilute clotting factors, cool the patient and raise BP enough to re-bleed

Shock with muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins, equal breath sounds after a stab wound:

flashcards.question: Shock types in trauma
flashcards.answer: Hypovolemic/hemorrhagic (commonest), obstructive (tension pneumothorax, tamponade), neurogenic (cord injury), cardiogenic (blunt cardiac injury).

flashcards.question: Compensated vs decompensated
flashcards.answer: Compensated (class I–II, up to 30%): BP held by tachycardia and vasoconstriction. Decompensated (class III–IV): hypotension, confusion.

flashcards.question: ATLS hemorrhage classes
flashcards.answer: I up to 15%; II 15–30% (tachycardia, BP maintained); III 31–40% (hypotension, confusion); IV more than 40% (pre-arrest).

flashcards.question: Permissive hypotension
flashcards.answer: Small boluses to a radial pulse or systolic 80–90 mmHg. Not with head injury: keep systolic at least 110 mmHg in most adults.

flashcards.question: Neurogenic vs hemorrhagic shock
flashcards.answer: Neurogenic: bradycardia, warm dry skin, cord injury. Hemorrhagic: tachycardia, cool pale clammy skin, bleeding.

flashcards.question: Prehospital fluid in hemorrhage
flashcards.answer: IV/IO en route; boluses of about 250 mL titrated to a radial pulse or systolic 80–90 mmHg; blood where available; avoid large crystalloid volumes.

flashcards.question: Tension pneumothorax vs tamponade
flashcards.answer: Tension: absent breath sounds one side, hyperresonance. Tamponade: equal breath sounds, muffled heart sounds. Both: distended neck veins, low BP.

flashcards.question: Prehospital shock care
flashcards.answer: Stop bleeding, oxygen to target, keep warm, pelvic binder if needed, permissive fluids, rapid transport, pre-alert.

critical.scenario: Gunshot to the right upper chest. At first BP 102/74, flat neck veins, clear breath sounds. Ten minutes later: BP 88/60, HR 130, SpO₂ 89%, distended neck veins, right chest hyperresonant with absent breath sounds.
critical.question: Cause of the sudden decline?

options.t: Tension pneumothorax: needle decompression (ALS) now, then rapid transport

options.f: Distended neck veins and hyperresonance point to tension.
Breath sounds are absent on one side.

critical.explanation: Adults: 4th or 5th intercostal space just in front of the mid-axillary line, or 2nd space mid-clavicular.
critical.kpi: Recognizes tension pneumothorax as obstructive shock

critical.scenario: A belted driver in a frontal crash: seat-belt bruise, epigastric tenderness. BP 100/68 at first; 15 minutes later 84/52, HR 126, confused, abdomen distending.
critical.question: Source and adjustment?

options.t: Intra-abdominal bleeding: small fluid boluses to systolic 80–90 mmHg, keep warm, update the trauma centre
Sit her up to stop vomiting
options.f: Keep her flat or on her side.

critical.explanation: The seat-belt sign is a red flag for liver, spleen and mesenteric injury.
critical.kpi: Recognizes progression to decompensated hemorrhagic shock

critical.scenario: Rollover: BP 88/56, HR 60, warm dry skin, thoracic spine tenderness, no sensation below the nipples, no leg movement.
critical.question: How do you tell neurogenic from hemorrhagic shock, and manage?

options.t: Neurogenic (warm, dry, slow pulse, cord injury): spinal motion restriction, fluids, ALS for vasopressors and atropine – and keep looking for bleeding
No treatment: it's just the spine
options.f: Low BP harms the injured cord.

critical.explanation: Both can coexist after a rollover.
